name: Egocentric Bias
description: Our own actions, effort, and reasons are more mentally available to us than other people's, so shared events can look more self-centered than they really were. People may overclaim their contribution or interpret the same history from a self-favoring vantage point.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to collaboration tools, shared-doc/workflow products, team retrospectives, attribution of project outcomes, co-creation features, and stakeholder debates about who did what. Participants can sincerely overestimate their own contribution because their own effort is easiest to recall.
myth_risk_note: 'Egocentric bias' as a label bundles several dissociable, separately well-documented phenomena -- false consensus, contribution overclaiming in joint work, and the spotlight effect -- under one umbrella term. The literature strongly supports each subtype individually, but treating them as a single unified mechanism risks overstating their coherence as one effect. The existing 'partial' status correctly reflects this.
prevalence_note: Shows up in collaboration, negotiation, and research-methods discussions, but designers more often invoke neighboring labels like self-serving bias, projection, or false consensus instead of this exact term.

findings.description: Across five experiments involving discussion groups, married couples, basketball teams, and laboratory groups, people's own contributions to a joint product were more available in memory than others' contributions, and they consequently claimed more responsibility for the shared outcome than other participants attributed to them. Making another participant's contributions more retrievable reduced this asymmetry, linking the overclaiming pattern to self-centered availability in memory rather than pure bad faith.
findings.source_title: Egocentric biases in availability and attribution.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
